title: Drum solos then and now; drums to be felt, not heard
summary: He explains that drum solos were rarely more than four bars and drummers were taught to stay below the piano.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Well, we might ask about drum solos and style of playing drums, the way it used to be and the way it is now. We only have another minute, unless you have something dictated. No, that's not.

Well, we, we, uh, uh, Baby Dodge was the drummer on the boat, you see. And Ray Badu, Leo Addy and myself, the three of us, we used to all go in there, we'd copy all the Baby's licks. So at that time, if you hear, if you heard any one of the three of us, you heard the same thing, because we all played the same, the same licks. But there was never any drum solos, Bill. You got two bars, you got four bars at the most. There was never anything more than, more than four bars. And that's, that's why I can't stand drum solos today.

Because we were, we were taught that the drums were supposed to be felt, not supposed to be heard. And if you played loud, they called you mule foot, you know. You wasn't, you wasn't supposed to play all that. Just loud as you could play. You were supposed to work for the band, instead of, uh, and you are, you had to be even, even, even below the piano, so the piano could be heard, you know. Yeah. So that you didn't interfere with it. As long as you didn't interfere with anybody, well then everything was fine.
